question: Why can history-dependent data-driven models predict partially observed physical systems, and how are they related to explicit physics models that assimilate missing state variables?

key_findings.claim: The optimal mean-square history-dependent predictor is a Wiener projection of Koopman evolution onto functions of observed delay coordinates.
key_findings.evidence: The paper connects conditional expectations, Hilbert-space target functions, and Mori-Zwanzig projection. Past observations enter through delay embeddings, implicitly representing missing degrees of freedom and the memory terms that instantaneous DMD/EDMD omit.

key_findings.claim: Maximum Caliber constructs observation-conditioned nonequilibrium measures and predictive distributions without assuming equilibrium.
key_findings.evidence: For a past of depth k, the allowed full states are the intersection of inverse images consistent with every observation. A uniform measure on that support is propagated by Perron-Frobenius evolution and pushed through the observable map; its expectation equals the nonequilibrium Wiener predictor.

anchors.section: B Maximum Caliber and C Predictive Distributions

key_findings.claim: Longer histories can shrink predictive uncertainty, but convergence to the true observed dynamics is conditional rather than universal.
key_findings.evidence: If dynamical refinement reduces the consistent-state support to one full state as k approaches infinity, predictive variance vanishes and the conditional mean becomes exact. The authors explicitly state this need not occur; generating partitions provide a rigorous special case and chaotic reverse-time contraction can help.

key_findings.claim: Delay histories recover full-state forecasting skill in a Lorenz-63 analog experiment.
key_findings.evidence: An instantaneous predictor using x alone diverges immediately, while an x-only delay embedding with dimension 7 and lag 4 forecasts essentially like the full (x,y,z) state, tracking for about four Lyapunov times.

key_findings.claim: On 50-dimensional Lorenz-96, increasing past depth substantially reduces analog-forecast error.
key_findings.evidence: For a single observed coordinate over 1,000 integration steps, MSE is 3.35 at k=3, 3.18 at k=20, 1.72 at k=80, and 0.15 at k=120, near the 2N+1 embedding heuristic.

method.core_idea: Express explicit state reconstruction and implicit history-based prediction as two ways of approximating the same partially observed dynamics.
method.mechanism: Define full 'Platonic' dynamics and observation maps; derive Koopman/Perron-Frobenius evolution, Mori-Zwanzig memory, delay embeddings, and equilibrium/nonequilibrium Wiener projections; use Maximum Entropy/Caliber support measures to form predictive distributions; analyze infinite-history refinement; illustrate with generating partitions and analog forecasts on Lorenz systems.
assumptions: A well-defined underlying dynamical system and observation map generate the data.
Relevant observables and conditional expectations lie in the chosen Hilbert spaces.
Past observations contain enough information to refine hidden-state uncertainty.
Data are sufficient to approximate the needed operator projections or analog neighborhoods.
The observation/support measures used by Maximum Caliber are appropriate least-biased choices.

techniques.role: Separates observable evolution from distribution evolution.
Shows why partial observation induces memory and orthogonal noise.
Defines the optimal history-dependent Hilbert-space predictor.
Builds nonequilibrium state uncertainty from observation histories.
Connects longer histories to smaller support and lower forecast variance.
Empirically tests hidden-state recovery through delays.

evaluations.result: Seven-delay x-only analog forecast is essentially as skillful as full-state forecast
MSE drops from 3.35 at depth 3 to 0.15 at depth 120
Support converges almost everywhere to a single state in the rigorous special case
Data assimilation and delay histories are shown as explicit and implicit hidden-state reconstruction

limitations: Most contributions are theoretical synthesis; numerical evidence uses low-dimensional canonical systems and simple analog forecasting.
Infinite-history convergence is explicitly not guaranteed for arbitrary observation maps or dynamics.
Finite data, noise, nonstationarity, irregular sampling, and model misspecification can prevent reliable conditional-expectation estimation.
The Maximum Caliber choice of uniform support measure may not reflect known nonuniform priors or measurement noise.
Delay dimension grows rapidly and creates severe sample-complexity and nearest-neighbor problems.
The framework explains prediction but does not automatically yield interpretable causal equations for hidden variables.
failure_modes: The observation map is non-generating, so distinct hidden states remain indistinguishable under every history.
Measurement noise makes support intersections empty or misleadingly diffuse.
Long delays create a curse of dimensionality and poor analog coverage.
Nonstationary dynamics invalidate a single Koopman/operator description.
Chaotic divergence limits useful forecast horizon even after state reconstruction.
A misspecified prior or support measure produces poorly calibrated predictive distributions.
reusable_insights: Model partial observation as a memory problem before selecting an architecture.
Evaluate whether adding history decreases calibrated predictive uncertainty, not merely training error.
Use explicit known physics for constraints and learn only unresolved components implicitly.
Distinguish state-reconstruction sufficiency from long-horizon predictability in chaotic systems.
Frame deterministic forecasts as expectations of predictive distributions so uncertainty remains visible.
open_questions: What finite-sample tests detect whether an observation history is approaching a generating representation?
How should noisy and irregular measurements modify Maximum Caliber support sets?
Can learned compact memories replace raw long delays while retaining operator guarantees?
How can hybrid models decide which physics to encode explicitly and which residual dynamics to learn?
What calibrated stochastic model best represents the remaining Mori-Zwanzig orthogonal component?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning reduced systems via deep neural networks with memory
competitive_landscape.difference: Fu, Chang, and Xiu discretize finite-memory MZ terms and learn them with a history-aware neural network. The reviewed paper supplies a broader operator/statistical-mechanics explanation and convergence conditions rather than a task-specific closure algorithm.

competitive_landscape.title: Chaos as an Intermittently Forced Linear System
competitive_landscape.difference: HAVOK uses Hankel delay coordinates to obtain an intermittently forced linear representation of chaos. Rupe et al. focus on optimal conditional prediction and how histories encode unobserved state through Wiener/Mori-Zwanzig projections.

competitive_landscape.title: The Mori-Zwanzig formulation of deep learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Venturi and Li formulate layerwise deep-network propagation itself through MZ memory and derive memory-decay conditions. The reviewed paper treats physical systems observed through measurements and explains why data-driven histories can recover hidden dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: Prediction and Retrodiction in Statistical Mechanics from the Principle of Maximum Caliber
competitive_landscape.difference: Tapia et al. derive predictive and retrodictive nonequilibrium models from path constraints. Rupe et al. use observation-conditioned MaxCal measures specifically to construct delay-based predictive distributions and operator projections for partial observation.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Nonequilibrium Maximum-Caliber Wiener projections unify implicit data-driven and explicit physics-based prediction for partially observed systems and explain possible convergence to true observable dynamics.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper integrates operator theory, projection formalism, predictive distributions, rigorous generating-partition intuition, and Lorenz demonstrations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The value is primarily conceptual synthesis and a precise probabilistic account of history. It does not make convergence generic or solve finite-data memory learning, but it supplies strong design and validation principles for hybrid forecasting.

reviewer_notes: Read all 29 extracted pages, including appendices on generating partitions, EDMD, and equations-from-data. Four primary arXiv competitors were checked on 2026-08-23. Operator identities were passage-checked but not independently rederived.
